rows.question: Where has Ben worked?
rows.answer: Ben has worked in three sectors across four roles [source: profile-summary]. His first role was as a Research Analyst at Technology Investment Network in New Zealand from November 2021 to June 2022, where he automated data collection in Python and produced analysis for published reports on the technology sector [source: role-tin]. He then worked in law at Russell McVeagh and in financial services at Visa, where he was an Associate Data Engineer from May 2024 to June 2026 [source: profile-summary, role-visa]. At Visa, his work spanned cloud infrastructure, ETL pipelines, dashboard development, and infrastructure migration [source: role-visa].
rows.context:
[source: role-tin] Ben's analyst role at Technology Investment Network
Ben was a Research Analyst at Technology Investment Network in New Zealand from November 2021 to
June 2022, his first role after graduating.

He automated the data-collection process in Python, replacing legacy Excel queries and manual
data entry, and produced the data analysis and written content that fed the published reports on
the New Zealand technology sector.

It is the smallest role on his CV and the one that set the pattern for the rest. The work he was
hired to do was largely manual assembly, and the useful contribution turned out to be removing
most of it rather than doing it faster. That is also where the writing half of the job came in.
The reports were published, so the analysis had to be defensible to readers who had never seen
the underlying data, which is close to the habit of documenting decisions and their rejected
alternatives that shows up throughout his later projects.

[source: profile-summary] Who Ben is, in one paragraph
Benjamin Best is a data engineer based in London, with the right to work in the UK. He is on a Youth Mobility Visa until June 2029. He has four
years of commercial experience across three sectors: financial services at Visa, law at Russell
McVeagh, and technology research at Technology Investment Network.

His range is deliberately end to end. At Visa he worked on cloud infrastructure and ETL at one
end and on the Power BI dashboards that surfaced the resulting data at the other, which is unusual
for a data engineering title and is the thread running through most of his work: he tends to own
a thing from the storage layer through to the screen a user actually looks at.

once, and the projects he builds in his own time tend to have the same shape.

[source: what-im-looking-for] What Ben is looking for next
Ben is targeting mid-level data engineering roles and junior software engineering roles, and
anything close to either. The software engineering side follows from roughly the last year at
Visa spent in a more software-focused position.

has enjoyed most has been end to end: owning something from the cloud infrastructure and the ETL
through to the interface that puts the result in front of a user. Roles that split those apart,
where the data lands in a warehouse and becomes someone else's problem, are a worse fit for him
than the title alone would suggest.

every significant decision has its rejected alternative recorded next to it, and he would rather
join somewhere that treats that as normal than somewhere it has to be argued for.

right to work in the UK without sponsorship for that period. Specifics about availability, notice

Ben was an Associate Data Engineer at Visa from May 2024 to June 2026, his most recent role and
the longest of his career so far.

The remit was broader than the title suggests. It covered four fairly distinct areas: a partner
billing data pipeline on AWS that he led as feature lead; the replacement of a legacy black-box
billing process with a transparent Spark SQL pipeline; the Qlik dashboard embedding layer of a

first two items are conventional data engineering, meaning ETL, warehousing and infrastructure as

multi-tenant .NET monolith.

[source: role-visa-billing-pipeline] The partner billing pipeline Ben led at Visa
As feature lead at Visa, Ben designed and delivered an AWS data pipeline producing monthly
billing and reporting data for eight banking partners.

The ETL ran on AWS Glue using PySpark. The infrastructure was provisioned with AWS CDK in
TypeScript, giving each partner its own S3 bucket, Glue job, KMS key and IAM role, so that the
isolation between partners was enforced by AWS permissions rather than by application logic.
Onboarding a further partner was a configuration change rather than a manual setup exercise.

how the pipeline was structured, how the partner boundary was drawn, and how the infrastructure
was expressed, then building it and seeing it into production.

reasoning behind the isolation model has its own entry in this corpus.

[source: visa-isolation-in-iam-not-code] Why partner isolation lived in IAM, not application code
On the partner billing pipeline at Visa, each of the eight banking partners got its own S3
bucket, Glue job, KMS key and IAM role. The alternative, and the one most teams reach for first,
is a shared bucket with a partner identifier on each row and application code that filters by it.

Ben drew the boundary in IAM and KMS instead, and the reason is what happens when someone is
wrong. If isolation is enforced in application code, then a mistaken join, a missing WHERE clause
or a mis-set variable puts one bank's billing data in another bank's report, and nothing stops
it, because the code has permission to read everything. If isolation is enforced in IAM, the same
mistake fails: the role cannot read the other bucket and the job errors instead of quietly
producing a wrong number.

The second half of the decision was defining it in AWS CDK rather than clicking it into the
console. That made onboarding a ninth partner a configuration change rather than a manual walk
through several services, and more importantly it made the isolation reviewable in a pull request
rather than trusted to whoever configured it last and remembered correctly.

The cost is more infrastructure objects to manage. At eight partners that was clearly worth it.

rows.question: Tell me about a bug he got wrong the first time.
rows.answer:
Ben debugged a data race condition in an async provisioning flow at Visa while he was the sole engineer maintaining Qlik during a company-wide migration [source: role-visa-solo-cover]. His first attempt used polling — repeatedly checking whether a resource was ready — which worked in testing but kept failing intermittently in practice [source: visa-polling-to-timestamp].

The problem was fundamental: polling answers whether something is ready *now*, but a race condition is a question about *ordering* — which event happened before the other. More frequent polling narrows the window but never closes it, so a symptom that gets rarer is easy to mistake for one that is gone [source: visa-polling-to-timestamp]. He replaced it with a timestamp-based heuristic that compared when things happened rather than sampling whether they had happened, which addressed the ordering directly [source: visa-polling-to-timestamp].

[source: askben-no-chunking] Why this widget has no chunking logic
There is no chunking code in this project. One markdown file is one chunk, and the corpus is
authored at chunk size, with each file deliberately written at roughly 150 to 320 words on a
single topic.

This declines the chunking problem rather than solving it. Splitting long documents well is
genuinely hard: fixed-size windows cut sentences in half, paragraph splits produce wildly uneven
chunks, and the overlap you add to compensate inflates the index and returns near-duplicate
results. None of that has to be solved if the source material never needs splitting.

Ben is direct about the limitation, because it is the obvious follow-up question. This does not
generalise. It works because the corpus is small, hand-written, and written specifically for this
purpose. The moment you point the system at documents you did not author, a PDF, a wiki export,
a set of transcripts, atomic authoring stops being available and a real chunking strategy becomes
unavoidable.

A test in the repository enforces the discipline by failing if any chunk exceeds 320 words, on
the reasoning that a 600-word chunk is a chunking problem wearing a disguise.

[source: how-i-work] How Ben works
A few habits show up across everything Ben builds, consistently enough to be worth stating as
practice rather than preference.

He works test-first. The test is written and watched to fail before the implementation exists,
because a test that has never been seen failing is a test whose behaviour is unverified rather
than confirmed. The question answering service producing this answer was built that way
throughout.

He treats a fix he cannot explain as unfinished. The race condition he debugged at Visa is the
example he uses: his first attempt made the symptom rarer without addressing the cause, and a
symptom that gets rarer is easy to mistake for one that is gone.

Every project runs lint, type checking and tests in CI on every pull request, and he works on
feature branches with pull requests rather than committing to the main branch, including on
repositories where he is the only contributor.

He writes decisions down with their rejected alternatives attached. Most entries in this corpus
take that form: the choice, the thing not chosen, and the condition under which the answer would
change. A decision recorded without its alternative is indistinguishable from a default, and the
most useful thing to know about any technical choice is what would have to be true for it to be
wrong.

[source: askben-no-vector-db] Why this widget has no vector database
This question answering service uses no vector database. There is no Pinecone, no Chroma, no
pgvector. Retrieval is either a BM25 score over the chunks or a numpy dot product against a
matrix of embeddings that is committed to the repository.

The corpus is around thirty chunks. Embedded at 1024 dimensions that is a matrix of roughly
thirty by one thousand and twenty-four floats, which is about 120 kilobytes and fits comfortably
in memory. A brute-force comparison against every chunk is a single matrix multiplication taking
well under a millisecond. Approximate nearest neighbour search exists to avoid comparing against
everything, and at this size comparing against everything is already the fast path.

So a vector database would be a network hop, an API key, a second thing that can be down, and an
index that can silently drift out of sync with the corpus, in exchange for solving a problem that
does not exist yet.

Ben is clear about where the answer changes. This holds while the corpus fits in memory and
rebuilding the index is cheap. Somewhere in the low tens of thousands of chunks, or as soon as
the corpus updates continuously rather than by a commit, the calculation inverts.

authoritative, in the sense that whatever it produced was by definition what the business had

explained. Reconciling against a system you cannot read means every discrepancy is a question

[source: askben-no-chunking] Why this widget has no chunking logic
There is no chunking code in this project. One markdown file is one chunk, and the corpus is
authored at chunk size, with each file deliberately written at roughly 150 to 320 words on a
single topic.

This declines the chunking problem rather than solving it. Splitting long documents well is
genuinely hard: fixed-size windows cut sentences in half, paragraph splits produce wildly uneven
chunks, and the overlap you add to compensate inflates the index and returns near-duplicate
results. None of that has to be solved if the source material never needs splitting.

Ben is direct about the limitation, because it is the obvious follow-up question. This does not
generalise. It works because the corpus is small, hand-written, and written specifically for this
purpose. The moment you point the system at documents you did not author, a PDF, a wiki export,
a set of transcripts, atomic authoring stops being available and a real chunking strategy becomes
unavoidable.

A test in the repository enforces the discipline by failing if any chunk exceeds 320 words, on
the reasoning that a 600-word chunk is a chunking problem wearing a disguise.

[source: askben-no-vector-db] Why this widget has no vector database
This question answering service uses no vector database. There is no Pinecone, no Chroma, no
pgvector. Retrieval is either a BM25 score over the chunks or a numpy dot product against a
matrix of embeddings that is committed to the repository.

The corpus is around thirty chunks. Embedded at 1024 dimensions that is a matrix of roughly
thirty by one thousand and twenty-four floats, which is about 120 kilobytes and fits comfortably
in memory. A brute-force comparison against every chunk is a single matrix multiplication taking
well under a millisecond. Approximate nearest neighbour search exists to avoid comparing against
everything, and at this size comparing against everything is already the fast path.

So a vector database would be a network hop, an API key, a second thing that can be down, and an
index that can silently drift out of sync with the corpus, in exchange for solving a problem that
does not exist yet.

Ben is clear about where the answer changes. This holds while the corpus fits in memory and
rebuilding the index is cheap. Somewhere in the low tens of thousands of chunks, or as soon as
the corpus updates continuously rather than by a commit, the calculation inverts.
